fatal_errors: The proposed Cu@Gr addition and spark-plasma sintering do not reconstruct the target intervention, which was liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
The initial material is misidentified as an existing W–Cu composite rather than the nominally equiatomic, dendritic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy used to generate the RHEA–Cu composite.

The proposed graphene-mediated interface and activated-sintering mechanism omit the target's selective Ti–Cu exchange, retention of W/Ta/V-rich ligaments, and formation of an approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.
No cited evidence supports improved performance of the Cu@Gr composite under irradiation; the cited studies support SPS densification and room-condition transport improvements only.

The irradiation conditions and failure mode are unspecified, whereas the target evidence was narrowly limited to 25 keV He+ swelling and blistering tests on precursor dendrites as a proxy, not on the finished composite.
explanation: This is a literature-supported alternative for improving conventionally sintered W–Cu: the cited Cu@Gr study directly supports 0.8 wt.% addition, SPS processing, increased densification, continuous Cu pathways, and an approximately 24.3% thermal-conductivity improvement. Its paired control and falsification rule are reasonably discriminating. However, it has almost no reconstruction agreement with the hidden target in precursor, intervention, processing, architecture, or mechanism. It also overextends evidence from SPS composites to high-temperature fusion service and irradiation stability without specifying temperature, particle energy, dose, or damage mode. The baseline is limited to undoped W–Cu and omits the target comparisons with WTaVTi, pure W, pure Cu, and conventional W–Cu. Boundaries are broad rather than evidence-based, and the claimed graphene intercalation and suppression of phase separation are less directly supported than the cited activated-sintering and tungsten-carbide mechanisms.
